summary: Discusses the goals of detecting network attachment in IPv6. When a host joins a new link, it needs to quickly work out whether it moved to a different network and whether its existing IP configuration is still valid. The memo describes what a solution should achieve. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you walk into a room, you quickly check if it is the same room as before. This memo explains what a computer needs to figure out when it plugs into a network, so it knows if its settings still work.

questions: how do mobile devices know if they moved networks
what are the goals of dna in ipv6
subtitle: Requirements for quick and safe IPv6 network re-attachment detection

tldr.problem: When a mobile host connects to a new network link, it does not know whether its existing IP address configuration is still valid or if it needs a new one. Detecting this quickly is essential for seamless mobility.
tldr.mechanism: A Detecting Network Attachment (DNA) scheme allows a host to rapidly determine whether it is on the same network as before by checking link identity using router advertisements and neighbor discovery messages.
tldr.outcome: DNA enables mobile devices to maintain ongoing sessions during handoff with minimal interruption, though implementations must carefully balance speed against security and signaling overhead.

facts.label: Link change detection
facts.value: Determines whether a host remains on the same IPv6 link or moved to a new one

facts.label: Typical delay
facts.value: Several seconds without optimization; 1.75 seconds average for periodic RA arrival

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Informational (defines goals and problems, not a protocol specification)

today: RFC 4135 is an Informational RFC that remains current. IPv6 handoff detection is essential for mobile devices. The goals outlined here have influenced the design of subsequent DNA specifications. Modern mobile operating systems use various techniques (link-layer events, rapid neighbor solicitation, DHCPv6 Rapid Commit) to approximate these goals, though no single RFC solution became universally adopted.

sections.title: The handoff problem in mobile networks
sections.content:
Mobile devices like laptops and smartphones frequently move between networks: from home WiFi to office WiFi, between cellular towers, or in and out of network range. When a device establishes a new link-layer connection (the radio association with a WiFi access point or cellular base station), it must determine whether this is a new network or the same network as before. This is called link change detection.

The stakes are high. If the device has moved to a new IPv6 subnet, its IP addresses are no longer valid, and it must acquire new ones before it can communicate. If the device incorrectly assumes it is on the same link when it has moved, packets will be misrouted and connections will drop. If the device incorrectly assumes it has moved when it has not, it will unnecessarily reconfigure, interrupting active calls or downloads. The process of Detecting Network Attachment (DNA) allows a host to quickly and reliably determine link identity so it can decide whether to reuse or replace its IP configuration.
sections.eli5: Imagine your phone connects to WiFi. It needs to figure out in the next few seconds: is this the same WiFi I just disconnected from, or a new one? If it is the same, my addresses still work. If it is new, I need new addresses. Getting this wrong breaks your calls.

sections.title: Why DNA is difficult
sections.content:
Three factors make link change detection challenging. First, wireless links have fuzzy boundaries. A device may be within range of multiple WiFi access points simultaneously, with signal strength fading and increasing as it moves. Unlike a wired connection where plugging into a port is a clear event, wireless attachment is gradual. A device may move away from one access point toward another, and link change is not instantaneous.

Second, router advertisements are imprecise. When a host connects and sends a Router Solicitation (RS) to discover the network, it receives a Router Advertisement (RA) message. The RA should contain prefixes that identify the link. However, routers may send different prefixes in unsolicited RAs than in solicited ones for efficiency. Two different routers on different networks can even have the same link-local address (unique only within a link). A host cannot reliably use a single RA to confirm it is on the same link as before.

Third, network delays are significant. A host must wait a random delay of 0 to 1 second before sending a Router Solicitation, and a router must wait 0 to 0.5 seconds before replying. Combined with the fact that periodic RAs arrive on average halfway through a random interval (about 1.75 seconds), the total delay to detect attachment can approach several seconds—long enough to drop a voice call or interrupt a download.
sections.eli5: Three problems: (1) wireless signals fade in and out—unclear when you really switched; (2) routers do not always send the same information, making the link identity fuzzy; (3) waiting for answers takes seconds, and every second counts for a phone call.

sections.title: Ten goals for DNA solutions
sections.content:
The RFC lists ten goals for any DNA scheme. The core goals are: (G1) detect link identity reliably to determine whether IP configuration is still valid; (G2) minimize latency so handoff is fast; and (G3) avoid false positives—if the host is still on the same link, do not trigger a reconfiguration.

Practical and efficiency goals include: (G4) minimize signaling so DNA does not flood the link with messages; (G5) reuse existing mechanisms like Router Solicitation and Neighbor Solicitation rather than inventing new ones; and (G6) use link-local scope messages (messages that do not cross routers) because if the link has changed, off-link communication may not work.

Security and compatibility goals are critical: (G7) be compatible with secure neighbor discovery (SEND, which authenticates routers); (G8) avoid introducing new security holes such as man-in-the-middle attacks or denial-of-service vulnerabilities; (G9) work with unmodified devices that do not support DNA; and (G10) handle multi-link scenarios where a host may perceive multiple routers on different links simultaneously (common in wireless).
sections.eli5: A good DNA solution should (1) get the answer right; (2) get it fast; (3) not break if the answer is 'same link'; (4) not waste bandwidth; (5) use messages that already exist; (6) work even if the network is down; (7) work with security; (8) not create new attacks; (9) work with old devices; and (10) handle multiple WiFi access points at once.

sections.title: Security trade-offs and threats
sections.content:
DNA is intimately tied to the Neighbor Discovery protocol, which is fundamental to IPv6. An attacker on a wireless link can jam signals, inject fake router advertisements, or replay old messages to trick a host into making the wrong decision. Without secure DNA, a malicious attacker could convince a host it moved to a different network (triggering unnecessary reconfiguration) or trick it into staying on the attacker's network (breaking connectivity).

For example, an attacker might send a spoofed Router Advertisement claiming a new set of prefixes to make the host think it moved. The host would then reconfigure, potentially joining the attacker's network instead. Conversely, an attacker on the real network could jam solicitations so the host never receives the correct RA, staying disconnected. Even worse, if a host adjusts its firewall settings based on which network it believes it is on, an attacker could disable the firewall by spoofing a home network.

The RFC emphasizes that DNA schemes must be compatible with Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) and must not introduce new attack vectors. Any reachability checks (such as pinging an off-link host to confirm connectivity) must be authenticated and checked for freshness to prevent replay attacks. Link-layer authentication (like WPA2) does not guarantee network-layer authentication, so additional safeguards are needed.
sections.eli5: An attacker on WiFi can lie about the network identity and trick your device into joining their network, or block your messages so you think you are disconnected. Security means making sure DNA uses trusted information and cannot be fooled by lies.

sections.title: Goals framework for future solutions
sections.content:
RFC 4135 does not specify a DNA protocol; instead, it provides a framework of goals that guide the design of DNA solutions. The document explicitly excludes the actual IP configuration procedure (like DHCP) from DNA's scope—DNA only determines whether reconfiguration is needed, not how to obtain the new configuration.

The RFC is focused on IPv6, as DNS and link change mechanics are different in IPv6 than in IPv4. The document references a companion work for IPv4 DNA. By laying out the goals, the RFC helps subsequent specifications (like RFC 6059, which came later with a more detailed scheme) balance the competing demands of speed, security, and compatibility.

This is an Informational RFC, providing requirements and context for implementers and future protocol designers. It remains relevant for any system that handles mobile IPv6 connectivity, as the fundamental challenges of quickly and securely determining network attachment remain unchanged.
sections.eli5: This memo does not say how to do DNA—it just lists what a good DNA solution should achieve. Future memos will describe the actual method. By writing down the goals first, engineers avoid building something that is fast but insecure, or secure but too slow.
